pillar_reactions.evidence: Delivered around his two stated constraints, time and gym avoidance — '30 minutes, three to four times a week. We're unlocking the joints, getting the pump, the cardio, all the stuff, building the muscle' — plus five to ten minutes of morning mobility framed against his 10 to 12 hours of sitting. His response was minimal: asked what questions he had, he said 'None', and asked for his thoughts, 'Sounds good.' The one place he engaged with substance was on volume, and he pushed back that it seemed too little: 'I don't see how you can do it in no less. I mean, that seems like not enough... I would think at least three times a week in a gym for an hour and a half.' The rep answered that well with 'Have you ever done a kettlebell workout? ... after 30 minutes, you'll be tired.'

The most carefully handled pillar on the call, and correctly so, since the prospect already has a dietitian producing results. The rep did not compete with him: 'you're working with a nutritionist. So what this will like, we're probably going to recommend you just stay with what the nutritionist is saying. Sounds like it's working.' He then positioned Trevor's role as principles for after that relationship ends — 'even if you stop with your dietician, like you can still continue eating in a way that's very sustainable.' The prospect accepted it and volunteered the exact want it targets: 'I'd love to get to a point where I didn't have to follow an app if I don't want to.' Deferring rather than displacing an incumbent adviser is good practice and worth propagating.

The only pillar that produced real enthusiasm, and the prospect identified it unprompted as the decisive feature: 'I guess the main thing is that the guy is going to make sure your form's proper, right? Actually watch videos of what you do and make sure that it's like, that you're not doing it wrong. I guess that's one of probably my main things about not going to the gym is not doing it right.' He then supplied his own proof from a directly analogous purchase: $2,500 for a year of his son's guitar lessons with weekly video submissions — 'he's held accountable. He sends in a video every week. It's unreal, the progress he's made... So I know it works, right? I do know it works.' That analogy was handed over and never used in the close.

anchors.raw: the only other person I've ever talked with, and we know actually, it's the $150,000 guy, right?… I think he wants like 12 grand, man. I think it's 12,000… I just didn't particularly care for the whole, you got to make this much money to do my program.
anchors.competitor: Unnamed 'superhuman guy' coach with a stated $150,000 income requirement, priced around $12,000
anchors.note: A rare doubly favourable anchor. It makes $6,000 look moderate at half the competing price, and the competitor's income-qualification gate is something the prospect actively disliked, which positions Primal as the more welcoming option. He has an indirect personal connection to that coach's operation through his wife's friend. The rep acknowledged it briefly and did not use either half.

anchors.raw: I just did this with my son on guitar. He's 13, about to be 14… I paid $2,500 for this kid to do guitar lessons for a year. And he's held accountable. He sends in a video every week. It's unreal, the progress he's made. And I just recently did this. Like, really recently did this. So I know it works, right? I do know it works.
anchors.note: The strongest anchor available on this call and the prospect built it himself. Same mechanism, video submission plus weekly feedback, same buyer, recent, and independently judged to have worked. He is effectively pricing the model at $2,500 a year for a child and considering $6,000 for six months for himself, which is the objection and the answer in the same breath. It was never referenced again.

anchors.raw: I got credit cards, but they get paid off every month, and I can't pay off a $6,000 bill in a month. I'd have to sell some stock.
anchors.note: Not an affordability problem — he paid cash for a $19,000 car for his daughter and $2,500 for guitar lessons — but a cash-timing one he has a firm personal rule about. This is the textbook case for an instalment structure and the fourth prospect in this batch to raise payment mechanics and be told most people pay upfront by card.

anchors.raw: I don't have to pay the dietician though. Fortunately, my insurance covers… And he's a good friend of mine, but I mean, he does get paid through my insurance. I guess it's a preventative thing or whatever.
anchors.note: His current, effective health coaching costs him nothing and is delivered by a friend who is also visibly fit and pushing him toward strength training. That sets a reference price of zero for professional health guidance and creates the risk that the dietitian simply absorbs the training role — a possibility the prospect raised out loud: 'or if he tells me, no, dummy, go do this, and you can come work out with me.'

unmet_demand.want: Something concrete to give his dietitian, whose endorsement he says would decide the purchase. He asked for it directly: 'is there anything I should share with him that would make him even think about doing that type of stuff himself or whatever?'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Nothing exists. The answer was 'Show him the videos and watch. That's probably what I'll do.' There is no methodology summary, no evidence document, no professional-facing material of any kind for a prospect to hand to a health adviser acting as gatekeeper. This is the second call in the corpus where a health professional stands between the prospect and the purchase and the rep has nothing to give them.

unmet_demand.want: Evidence that the programme works for someone at his starting point. He raised it himself and accurately: 'one thing with his before and after is, though, I didn't see no fat people, you know, that do this. I didn't see any fat, like, fat, fat people.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Answered by assertion rather than evidence — 'we've had a, definitely a, I mean, it's just not the ones we advertise the most' — followed by a redirect casting him as the ideal client. The marketing observation he made is correct on its face and the counter-claim is unverifiable from anything he was shown. Left unvalidated because the call gives no basis to judge whether such clients exist.

unmet_demand.want: A payment structure that does not require liquidating stock. Asked in substance — 'And that's $1,000 a month? How do you pay that? Up front?'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Told 'most people just put in a credit card and pay it up front', with no mention that instalment options exist. They demonstrably do — internal calls the previous day put average upfront collection at about $4,000 against a $6,000 price and describe two-pay structures and a $1,200 entry tier. The one commercial answer that fit this prospect's stated constraint was never put to him.

unmet_demand.want: Programming that uses his continuous glucose monitor and A1C data. He wears a CGM, logs everything, sends it to his dietitian weekly and gets adjustments — 'I would document everything that would spike my... And then I would send it to him, and then he would tweak it the next week.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Never addressed. Progress tracking was described as workouts, weight and photos. For a prospect whose entire goal is a glycaemic marker and who already runs a weekly data-and-adjust loop with someone else, connecting the programme to that loop was the natural bridge and it was never attempted.

unmet_demand.want: Confidence that he can train safely having done no resistance work since high school, which he named as the single thing that stood out about the offer.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Partly served and well served — the form-review mechanism is exactly the answer and he responded to it more strongly than to anything else. Recorded here because the other half of that want went unmet: nobody asked whether he had any injuries or physical limitations, and nobody suggested that a 49-year-old diabetic, sedentary for fifteen years, might want clinical clearance before starting loaded ballistic training.
